_comment: DBE Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2024. Questions + marking-memo
answers extracted by reading the rendered scanned question paper (no text layer)
and the bilingual (Afrikaans/English) Marking Guidelines PDF (text layer present).
Only the ENGLISH memo content is transcribed. solution_method is the method the
MEMO uses to solve each question - this is the content signal the matcher links
against, not the surface wording of the question. memo_answer is verbatim from
the guidelines (decimal commas kept, South African convention).
CONTEXT CONVENTION: Mathematical Literacy questions hang off shared scenario/
resource boxes. The full scenario (tables/plans/pictures described in bracketed
words) is transcribed verbatim inside the text of the FIRST sub-question of each
block, prefixed 'CONTEXT for ...'. Later sub-questions carry a short pointer.
ANNEXURE NOTE: The paper references an ADDENDUM with ANNEXURES A-C (campsite
aerial view, Leopard Trail Run map + elevation map, Australia map/trip plan).
The addendum PDF is NOT in this directory; annexure descriptions below are
reconstructed from the values the marking guidelines use, and are marked
_note_binaries: Both scanned PDFs are committed in this directory (paper2.pdf = question paper, paper2_memo.pdf = bilingual marking guidelines). The addendum (3 annexures) is not in the repo.

questions.text: CONTEXT for 3.1 (Q3.1.1-3.1.3): Mrs Kgomo is a Grade 2 teacher at Happy Valley Primary School. She has a reading corner at the back of her classroom. Learners who wait for their transport after school, usually sit there and read a book. Mrs Kgomo stores pillows in bags (see pictures below). Learners sit on these pillows after school. [Two-panel figure: photo of pillows in a zip-up storage bag with piping labelled; diagram of the bag with dimensions 46 cm long, 30 cm wide, 48 cm high. NOTE: Piping: thin cord covered in fabric used to decorate the bag and reinforce the seams.] [Adapted from www.shein.com] Use the information above to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: The school day ends at 12:55. Tendani's father was late and only came to fetch him at 14:13. Determine how long Tendani sat in the reading corner.
questions.memo_working: = 14:13 - 12:55 (1MA subtracting time) = 1 hour 18 minutes (1A simplification). AO

questions.text: [Context 3.1: pillow storage bags - see Q3.1.1] The height of one pillow is 11 cm. Determine the difference between the total height of the pillows in ONE bag and the height of the bag. [The bag diagram shows 4 pillows stacked in the bag.]
questions.memo_working: Total height of 4 pillows = 11 cm x 4 (1MA multiplying by 4) = 44 cm (1CA). Difference = 48 cm - 44 cm (1RT height) = 4 cm (1CA simplification). OR 48 - 11 - 11 - 11 - 11 = 4 cm. AO

questions.text: [Context 3.1: pillow storage bags - see Q3.1.1] The piping around the bottom edge of some of the bags for the pillows needs to be replaced. The store sells the piping in half-metre lengths. Calculate the total length of piping she will have to purchase to replace the piping around the bottom edges of FOUR bags. You may use the following formula: Perimeter = 2 (length + width)
questions.memo_answer: 6,5 m (i.e. 13 half-metre lengths; 4 bags need 6,08 m)
questions.memo_working: Perimeter = 2(46 cm + 30 cm) (1SF correct substitution) = 2(76 cm) = 152 cm (1CA). Total for 4 bags = 152 x 4 (1MA multiply by 4) = 608 cm = 6,08 m (1C simplification); she must buy 6,5 m (1R correct rounding). OR converting to metres first: 2(0,3 + 0,46) = 1,52 m; x 4 = 6,08 m; buy 6,5 m. OR 608 cm ÷ 50 cm = 12,16 ≈ 13 half-metre lengths (1R correct rounding)

questions.text: CONTEXT for 3.2 (Q3.2.1-3.2.3): Mrs Kgomo created a birthday calendar for her 2024 class to hang against the wall. She will write each learner's name and birthday on a small circular wooden tag and attach the tag to the correct month. The circular wooden tag has a circular hole to attach a ring that is used to hang the tag. The area of the circular hole is 0,3142 cm^2. Every year she paints the front surface area of the circular wooden tags. The spread rate of the paint is 6 m^2/l. [PICTURE AND DIAGRAM OF A CIRCULAR WOODEN TAG: photo of a round tag reading 'Annette 6 April' with the circular hole arrowed; diagram of a circle 8 cm high and 8 cm wide with a small hole at the top.] [Adapted from www.amazon.com] Use the information above to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Determine, in cm, the circumference of the circular wooden tag. You may use the following formula: Circumference of a circle = 3,142 x diameter
questions.memo_working: Circumference = 3,142 x 8 cm (1SF substitute diameter) = 25,136 cm (1A simplification). NPR, AO

questions.text: [Context 3.2: circular wooden tags - see Q3.2.1] Determine, in cm, the radius of ONE circular wooden tag.
questions.memo_working: Radius = 8 cm / 2 (1MA concept of radius) = 4 cm (1A simplification). NPU, AO

questions.text: [Context 3.2: circular wooden tags - see Q3.2.1] The hardware store sells paint in 50 ml, 1 litre, 5 litre and 20 litre containers. Mrs Kgomo claims that a 50 ml can of paint will be sufficient to paint ONE side of 36 circular wooden tags. Verify her statement. Show ALL calculations. Use the following formula: Area of a circle = 3,142 x radius^2
questions.memo_answer: Area per tag = 3,142 x 4^2 = 50,272 cm^2; minus hole = 49,9578 cm^2; 36 tags = 1 798,4808 cm^2 = 0,17984808 m^2; paint needed = 0,17984808/6 l ≈ 30 ml, which is less than 50 ml. Her statement is VALID (50 ml is more than sufficient).
questions.memo_working: Area of a circle = 3,142 x (4 cm)^2 (1SF correct substitution) = 3,142 x 16 cm^2 (1MCA squaring) = 50,272 cm^2 (1CA). Area to be painted = 50,272 - 0,3142 = 49,9578 cm^2 (1CA difference). Total area = 36 x 49,9578 cm^2 = 1 798,4808 cm^2 (1MCA multiply by 36) = 1 798,4808 ÷ 100^2 = 0,179848 m^2 (1C dividing by 10 000). 6 m^2 = 1 l = 1 000 ml; 50 ml covers 0,3 m^2 (1MA using ratio); 0,3 m^2 > 0,179848 m^2 (1CA comparing areas). Therefore 50 ml will be more than sufficient (1O verification). OR paint needed = 0,17984808/6 = 0,02997466 l ≈ 30 ml; VALID.

questions.text: CONTEXT for 3.3 (Q3.3.1-3.3.2): On each learner's birthday, the learner receives a cubic-shaped packet of homemade sweets, as shown in the diagram and picture below. [DIAGRAM AND PICTURE OF A CUBE AND A CUBIC-SHAPED PACKET: line drawing of a cube; photo of a cube-shaped gift packet with handles.] [Adapted from www.pinterest.com] Use the diagram above to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: The volume of the cubic-shaped packet is 2 744 cm^3. Calculate the side length of the cubic-shaped packet. You may use the following formula: Volume of a cube = side x side x side
questions.memo_working: 2 744 cm^3 = side x side x side (1SF substitution number, 1SF cube unit); (side)^3 = 2 744 cm^3 (1MA change subject of the formula); 14 x 14 x 14 = 2 744; side = 14 cm (1CA simplification)

questions.text: [Context 3.3: cubic-shaped sweet packets - see Q3.3.1] There are 35 different coloured sweets in each packet. TABLE 2 below shows the number of sweets per colour. [TABLE 2: NUMBER OF SWEETS PER COLOUR. Blue 4; Purple 5; Pink 8; Orange 11; Yellow 7.] Determine the probability, as a decimal, of randomly choosing a pink or a yellow sweet from the packet.

CONTEXT for 4.1 (Q4.1.1-4.1.4): Crude oil is heated in a vertical, cylindrical tower to separate and extract products, such as petroleum gas, gasoline (petrol), kerosene (lamp oil), diesel, industrial oil, and paraffin wax, which boil at different temperatures. [Two-panel figure. Left: cylindrical tower showing different products and their boiling temperatures - petroleum gas 20 °C at the top, then gasoline (petrol) 150 °C, kerosene (lamp oil) 200 °C, diesel 300 °C, industrial oil 370 °C, paraffin wax 400 °C at the bottom; extractor pipes lead off each level and a furnace feeds the tower. Right: diagram of a vertical, cylindrical tower with domed top section A, cylindrical middle section B of height 54 m, domed bottom section C, and diameter 6 m.] NOTE: Extraction occurs because different liquids have different boiling points. Extraction takes place in a large, vertical, cylindrical tower with a diameter of 6 m. The total surface area of sections (A + C) = 150,816 m^2. [Adapted from http://derivfx.com] Use the information above to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Identify the crude oil product that will be third to boil.
questions.memo_working: 2RT correct product

questions.text: [Context 4.1: crude oil distillation tower - see Q4.1.1] Write down the product extracted at 150 °C.
questions.memo_working: 2RT correct product

questions.text: [Context 4.1: crude oil distillation tower - see Q4.1.1] Convert the boiling point of diesel to degrees Fahrenheit. Use the formula: °C = (°F - 32) / 1,8
questions.memo_working: 300 °C = (°F - 32)/1,8 (1RT correct value 300, 1SF substituting information correctly); °F = 1,8 x 300 + 32 (1S changing subject of the formula) = 572 (1CA simplification). AO

questions.text: [Context 4.1: crude oil distillation tower - see Q4.1.1] The pipes leading in and out of the vertical, cylindrical tower take up 2,5% of the surface area of part B of the cylindrical tower. Calculate the total surface area of the vertical, cylindrical tower, excluding the area taken up by the pipes. Use the formula: Surface area of an open cylinder = 3,142 x diameter x height
questions.topic: Measurement (surface area of a cylinder, percentage)
questions.memo_working: SA = 3,142 x 6 m x 54 m (1SF substitution) = 1 018,008 m^2 (1CA). Area of pipes = 2,5/100 x 1 018,008 (1MCA percentage calculation) = 25,4502 m^2 (1CA). Total = 1 018,008 - 25,4502 + 150,816 (1MCA subtracting pipe area, 1MA adding A + C) = 1 143,3738 m^2 (1CA total surface area). OR area excluding pipes = 97,5/100 x 1 018,008 = 992,5578 m^2; + 150,816 = 1 143,3738 m^2. NPR

questions.text: CONTEXT for 4.2 (Q4.2.1-4.2.3): A worker at the oil refinery intends converting her double-door garage into a bigger living room by building double-bricked walls to replace both of the doors. [Four-panel figure: photo of the two garage doors to be replaced; photo of bricks stacked on a wooden pallet; incomplete diagram showing the pattern of how the bricks should be laid, with the first two rows completed - the bottom row shows 9 full bricks and a half brick, and the wall is 20 rows high in the side view; side view of the double-brick wall showing two brick thicknesses.] NOTE: 525 bricks per pallet at a price of R6,45 per brick. Bricks are sold per pallet. Half bricks are thrown away (not re-used). Use the information above to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Determine the total number of pallets of bricks needed to replace both garage doors.
questions.memo_working: Number of bricks in 1 row of a double brick wall = 19 (2RT bricks in double row). Bricks for 1 garage door = 19 x 20 (1A number of layers) = 380. Total = 380 x 2 (1MCA doubling) = 760; therefore 2 pallets (1R number of pallets). OR single line wall = 20 x 10 = 200 bricks; double line wall = 2 x 200 = 400; both doors = 2 x 400 = 800; 2 pallets needed.
questions.memo_note: The two memo alternatives count 760 (19 bricks per double row, half bricks discarded) or 800 (10 per single row incl. half brick) bricks; both round to 2 pallets.

questions.text: [Context 4.2: double-brick garage walls - see Q4.2.1] The opening of a garage door has dimensions of 2,13 m x 3 m. Other costs to build the double-brick wall: Material, other than bricks, cost R2 000,00; Labour is R500,00 per square metre. The owner states that the total cost to replace both garage doors with walls would be R15 200,00. Verify her statement by means of calculations. You may use the following formula: Area = length x width
questions.memo_answer: Area of 2 doors = 12,78 m^2; labour = R6 390; bricks (2 pallets) = R6 772,50; total = R2 000 + R6 390 + R6 772,50 = R15 162,50. Her statement is NOT VALID.
questions.memo_working: Area of 2 doors = 2 x 2,13 x 3 (1MA doubling, 1SF correct values) = 12,78 m^2 (1A). Labour cost = 12,78 x R500 = R6 390 (1CA). Brick cost = 2 x 525 x R6,45 = R6 772,50 (1CA). Total cost = R2 000 + R6 390 + R6 772,50 = R15 162,50 (1CA amount). Not VALID (1O verification). CA pallets from 4.2.1. [Third memo alternative rounds area to 13 m^2, giving labour R6 500 and total R15 272,50 - also Not VALID.]

questions.text: [Context 4.2: double-brick garage walls - see Q4.2.1] Give ONE suitable reason why the bricks have to be placed on a wooden pallet.
questions.memo_answer: To be easily lifted by a fork lift. OR Storage/loading/transportation are made easier. OR It keeps them from breaking. OR It makes counting easier. OR To protect the bricks from damage. OR To keep it tight and compact.
questions.memo_working: 2O reason

questions.text: CONTEXT for 5.2 (Q5.2.1-5.2.2): Chris and Boipelo plan to visit Uluru. This oval-shaped big rock rises 1 142 feet above the surrounding desert plain. A picture of Uluru is shown alongside. The diagram below shows a comparison of the height of Uluru and some other tourist attractions around the world. [Diagram: outline of Uluru with heights marked - Sydney Harbour Bridge 134 m; ULURU 348 m; The Eiffel Tower 324 m; The Great Pyramid of Giza 139 m; Big Ben 96 m.] [Sources: Pinterest.com.au and Britannica.com] Use the information above to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Determine, rounded to THREE decimal places, the conversion factor from feet to metres used in this diagram, in the form 1 foot = ... m.
[Context 5.2: Uluru height comparison diagram - see Q5.2.1] Write, as a simplified ratio, the heights of Uluru : Eiffel Tower : Big Ben.
questions.memo_working: 348 : 324 : 96 (1RT correct values, 1A correct order) = 29 : 27 : 8 (2CA simplified ratio)

questions.text: CONTEXT for 5.3 (Q5.3.1-5.3.3): In addition to the mainland, Australia is surrounded by many thousands of small islands. Boipelo found TABLE 3 indicating the areas for the mainland, islands and total for each state or territory on a website. Some values have been omitted. [TABLE 3: AREA SIZES OF THE MAINLAND, ISLANDS AND TOTAL FOR EACH STATE OR TERRITORY. Columns: STATE/TERRITORY | MAINLAND AREA km^2 | ISLAND AREA km^2 | TOTAL AREA km^2 | PERCENTAGE OF TOTAL AREA. Rows: Western Australia 2 526 924 | 3 089 | 2 527 013 | 32,9; Queensland 1 723 030 | 6 712 | 1 729 742 | 22,5; Northern Territory 1 334 404 | 13 387 | 1 347 791 | 17,5; South Australia 979 651 | 4 670 | 984 321 | 12,8; New South Wales 801 137 | 13 | 801 150 | 10,4; Victoria 227 038 | 406 | 227 444 | 3,0; Tasmania 64 519 | 3 882 | 68 401 | 0,9; Australian Capital Territory 2 358 | - | 2 358 | -; TOTAL (AUSTRALIA) 7 656 061 | 32 159 | 7 688 220 | ... ] NOTE: Territory - a big area that compares to a district or province. [Source: ga.gov.au] Use TABLE 3 and refer to ANNEXURE C to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: A meteorite (rock from the sky) fell somewhere in Australia. Write down the probability that it randomly fell in Queensland.

[Context 5.3: TABLE 3 Australian area sizes - see Q5.3.1] Show, with calculations, why it could be stated that the total area of the islands of Australia is approximately half of the area of the mainland area of Tasmania.
questions.memo_working: Area of islands / area of Tasmania = 32 159/64 519 (1RT area of islands, 1RT area of Tasmania) = 0,498 ≈ 0,5 (1CA simplification). OR half of Tasmania = 64 519 x 1/2 = 32 259,5 km^2 vs islands 32 159 km^2. OR 64 519 : 32 159 ≈ 2 : 1

questions.text: [Context 5.3: TABLE 3 Australian area sizes - see Q5.3.1] The Australian Capital Territory has a population of 454 499. (a) Determine, rounded to the nearest whole number, the population density of the Australian Capital Territory as people per square km.
questions.memo_working: Population density = 454 499/2 358 (1RT correct 454 499, 1RT correct area 2 358) = 192,74... ≈ 193 (1R simplification rounded up)

questions.text: [Context 5.3: TABLE 3 Australian area sizes - see Q5.3.1] (b) Give a suitable reason, with calculations, why this area is omitted from the percentage calculation in the table.
questions.memo_answer: ACT % of total area = 2 358/7 688 220 x 100% = 0,0306...%, which rounds off to zero.
questions.memo_working: Land % area = 2 358/7 688 220 x 100% (1RT correct 2 358, 1RT 7 688 220) = 0,0306..% (1CA simplification). Rounds off to zero (1O opinion)
